prompt: What is the legal function of a bug bounty program's 'safe harbor' clause?
choices: It guarantees the researcher a financial reward regardless of severity
It grants advance authorization for good-faith testing within the program's defined scope, so that activity is not 'unauthorized access' under laws like the CFAA
It transfers all legal liability for any damage caused to the researcher onto the program
It allows the researcher to test any system owned by the company, whether listed in scope or not

prompt: Under a HackerOne Gold Standard Safe Harbor style policy, what must a researcher do to remain within the program's authorization while testing?
choices: Act in good faith, stay within the documented scope and technique restrictions, and avoid privacy violations or service disruption
Test any subdomain discovered via OSINT, whether or not it is listed in scope
Publicly disclose the finding immediately upon discovery to maximize attention
Run an automated scanner at full throughput with no rate limiting

prompt: In the CVSS 3.1 vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:C/C:H/I:L/A:N, what does the S:C component mean?
choices: The vulnerable component and the impacted component differ (Scope Changed)
The attack requires physical access to the target (Scope Confined)
The vulnerability has been confirmed by a triager (Scope Closed)
The maximum possible severity score is capped at this value (Scope Ceiling)

prompt: Why is checking for duplicate reports before submitting important in bug bounty work?
choices: Programs typically pay only the first qualifying report of a given root cause; later duplicates are closed as N/A with no payout
Duplicate reports are automatically merged and both researchers split the bounty evenly
A program requires at least three independent duplicate reports before it will triage an issue
Duplicate checking is unnecessary because triagers always perform it on the researcher's behalf before review

prompt: What should the 'Steps to Reproduce' section of a professional vulnerability report contain?
choices: A general description of the vulnerability class affected
Exact numbered steps with the actual request/response data and payload used, sufficient for a triager to reproduce the bug independently
Only a screenshot showing the final impact, without reproduction detail
A link to a generic OWASP article describing the vulnerability class

prompt: Why can DVWA and Juice Shop findings be used to practice HackerOne-style report writing but not actually be submitted to a live bug bounty program?
choices: They are intentionally vulnerable local training applications with no owner granting live-testing authorization or paying bounties, so they're used for practicing technique and report format, not submission
They are automatically in scope for every HackerOne program by default
They can be submitted to Bugcrowd as zero-day findings for a cash reward
They are production SaaS products operated directly by OWASP

prompt: What is a key structural difference commonly seen between HackerOne and Bugcrowd regarding how severity is rated?
choices: HackerOne programs commonly rate severity using CVSS, while Bugcrowd maintains its own Vulnerability Rating Taxonomy (VRT) that many of its programs use instead
Both platforms use an identical proprietary scoring system with no meaningful difference
Neither platform supports any form of severity rating for submitted reports
Only Bugcrowd supports CVSS scoring; HackerOne has no severity model at all

prompt: A researcher discovers an issue on an asset owned by the same company running a bug bounty program, but that asset is not listed on the program's scope page. What is the correct action?
choices: Test it anyway, since it belongs to the same company running the program
Do not test it; assets outside the documented scope are not covered by safe harbor, and testing them can constitute unauthorized access
Submit a report for it immediately, since demonstrated impact matters more than scope
Test it first, then ask the triager for retroactive permission afterward
